title: The Patient Art of Diplomacy
text:
Diplomacy is often imagined as a dramatic affair of summits, handshakes and signed treaties. In reality, most of its work is slow, unglamorous and conducted far from the cameras. Envoys spend months exchanging drafts, testing phrases and learning which concessions the other side can accept without appearing to surrender. A single agreement may rest on hundreds of conversations that the public never hears about.

The first quality a diplomat needs is not cleverness but patience. Governments rarely change their positions quickly, because every shift must be explained to parliaments, newspapers and citizens at home. A negotiator who pushes too hard for an immediate result may win a promise that collapses as soon as it meets domestic opposition. The skilled envoy therefore aims for agreements that each side can defend in its own capital.

The second quality is the ability to listen. Nations often state their demands in public language that hides their real concerns. A country that insists on a particular boundary line may actually be worried about access to water or the safety of a minority living near the border. By identifying these underlying interests, a patient diplomat can sometimes find solutions that neither side had considered at the start.

None of this makes diplomacy weak. A settlement reached through careful bargaining usually lasts longer than one imposed by force, because the parties have a stake in keeping it. The quiet work of envoys may never make headlines, yet it prevents far more conflicts than the public ever sees resolved.

title: The Limits of Economic Sanctions
text:
When one state wishes to change the behaviour of another without going to war, it often turns to economic sanctions. By restricting trade, freezing financial assets or banning the sale of certain goods, the sanctioning state hopes to raise the cost of the target’s policies until its leaders decide to change course. Sanctions appeal to politicians because they signal disapproval firmly while avoiding the loss of life that military action brings.

Their record, however, is mixed. A government that controls the media and faces no free elections can often shift the burden of sanctions onto ordinary people while its own elite remains comfortable. Shortages of medicine and food may then harm the very citizens whom the sanctions were meant to help, and the ruling group may even use the hardship to rally the public against foreign enemies.

Sanctions also tend to leak. If only a few countries impose them, the target can often find other buyers for its exports and other suppliers for its imports. Over time, new trading routes and informal markets develop, and the pressure that seemed overwhelming at the start gradually weakens.

For these reasons, many analysts now favour narrower measures aimed at specific individuals, companies or goods rather than at whole economies. Such targeted sanctions are harder to design and enforce, but they reduce harm to the general population. Even so, sanctions work best as one part of a wider strategy that includes negotiation and offers the target a clear path to having the measures lifted.

title: The City That Grew Too Fast
text:
Across much of the developing world, cities are growing faster than any plan can follow. Every year, families leave their villages in search of work, schooling and hospitals, and many of them settle wherever they can find space: on the edge of a railway line, beside a drain, or on hillsides no planner would have chosen. Within a few years, a patch of empty land can become a crowded neighbourhood with its own shops, mosques and schools, yet without paved roads, piped water or proper sewers.

It is tempting to treat such settlements as a problem to be cleared away. That view overlooks their strengths. Informal neighbourhoods are often dense, lively and economically productive; they house the cooks, drivers, builders and cleaners on whom the rest of the city depends. Demolishing them rarely makes poverty disappear. More often it simply moves poor families to another unserviced patch of land, usually further from their places of work.

A more promising approach is to improve these areas where they stand. When residents are given secure title to their homes, they tend to invest their own savings in stronger walls, better roofs and small businesses. When the city lays water pipes and drains along existing lanes, disease falls and the value of property rises. Such upgrading is slower and less dramatic than building new housing blocks, but it respects the communities people have already made.

The deeper lesson is that urban growth cannot be stopped by decree. Cities that plan ahead, setting aside land for roads and services before settlement arrives, spend far less than those that must repair the damage afterwards.

title: In Praise of Maintenance
text:
Politicians love to open things. A new bridge, a new motorway or a new hospital wing offers a ribbon to cut and a plaque bearing an official’s name. Nobody, by contrast, holds a ceremony when a drain is cleared, a pothole is filled or a water pipe is quietly replaced before it bursts. Yet it is this unnoticed work of maintenance that decides whether infrastructure serves the public for decades or crumbles within a few years.

The neglect is understandable but costly. Budgets for upkeep are the first to be cut when money is short, because their absence is not felt immediately. A road left unrepaired for one season still carries traffic; a pump station that misses its servicing still works, for a while. The damage accumulates silently until a small crack becomes a collapsed culvert, and the eventual bill is many times larger than the cost of timely repair.

There is also a human cost. Poorly maintained roads cause accidents, leaking pipes allow contaminated water to enter homes, and hospitals with broken equipment turn patients away. Those who suffer most are usually the poor, who cannot afford private alternatives.

A sensible government would reverse its priorities. Before announcing another grand project, it should ask whether it can afford to look after what it already has. Engineers should be rewarded for keeping systems running, not only for designing new ones, and every budget should set aside a fixed share for upkeep. Maintenance will never win elections on its own, but a country that ignores it will keep paying for the same infrastructure twice.

subject: English
q: The central idea of the passage is that diplomacy:
o: depends chiefly on dramatic summits and public ceremonies
succeeds mainly through patient and largely unseen negotiation
is a weak substitute for the use of force
works best when quick results are demanded
explanation: The passage contrasts the dramatic image of diplomacy with its real work: slow, patient negotiation conducted far from the cameras.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, why do governments rarely change their positions quickly?
o: Their envoys lack the authority to agree to anything
Every shift has to be explained to audiences at home
International law forbids sudden changes of policy
Foreign newspapers criticise every concession
explanation: The second paragraph says every shift must be explained to parliaments, newspapers and citizens at home.

subject: English
q: The example of a country that insists on a particular boundary line is used to show that:
o: border disputes can never be settled by negotiation
water is the most common cause of war between nations
minorities should always be moved away from borders
a public demand may conceal a different underlying concern
explanation: The author gives the example to show that nations state demands in public language that hides their real concerns, such as water or the safety of a minority.

subject: English
q: The word ‘concessions’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: formal complaints made against another state
secret reports sent to a government
things given up in order to reach an agreement
public celebrations of a signed treaty
explanation: Envoys learn which concessions the other side can accept “without appearing to surrender”, so concessions are things yielded to reach agreement.

subject: English
q: The author would most likely judge the success of diplomacy by:
o: how long its agreements last and how many conflicts it prevents
the number of summits held in a year
the amount of publicity its agreements receive
the speed with which each negotiation is concluded
explanation: The final paragraph values settlements that last longer and notes that diplomacy prevents far more conflicts than the public sees, while the passage dismisses publicity and speed.

subject: English
q: The author’s attitude towards the work of diplomats can best be described as:
o: mocking and dismissive
neutral and indifferent
anxious and pessimistic
respectful and appreciative
explanation: The author praises the patience and listening of diplomats and insists that their quiet work is not weak but prevents conflicts.

subject: English
q: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?
o: Why Sanctions Often Fall Short of Their Aims
How Sanctions Have Replaced War Altogether
The History of International Trade Routes
Why Sanctions Always Punish Governments
explanation: The passage examines why sanctions have a mixed record: their burden falls on ordinary people and they tend to leak.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, sanctions appeal to politicians because they:
o: express firm disapproval without the loss of life that war causes
guarantee a quick change in the target’s policies
are easy to design and cheap to enforce
are always supported by every other country
explanation: The first paragraph says sanctions signal disapproval firmly while avoiding the loss of life that military action brings.

subject: English
q: The passage says that sanctions ‘leak’ when:
o: the sanctioning state reveals its plans in advance
the target finds other trading partners and informal markets
ordinary citizens protest against their own government
targeted measures are replaced by broader ones
explanation: The third paragraph explains that the target can find other buyers and suppliers, and new routes and informal markets develop.

subject: English
q: The word ‘rally’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: calm down
divide into factions
question openly
unite in support
explanation: The ruling group uses hardship to rally the public against foreign enemies, that is, to bring people together behind it.

subject: English
q: It can be inferred from the passage that sanctions are most likely to succeed when:
o: a single country imposes them on a whole economy
many countries apply them and the target is offered a way to have them lifted
they are designed to cause maximum hardship to ordinary people
they replace negotiation entirely
explanation: The passage says sanctions leak when only a few countries impose them, and that they work best alongside negotiation with a clear path to their removal.

subject: English
q: The tone of the passage is best described as:
o: angry and accusatory
enthusiastic and promotional
humorous and light-hearted
balanced and analytical
explanation: The author weighs the appeal of sanctions against their weaknesses and considers alternatives without taking an emotional stance.

subject: English
q: The main idea of the passage is that informal settlements should be:
o: improved where they stand rather than demolished
cleared to make way for new housing blocks
left entirely to their residents without city support
moved far away from the centres of cities
explanation: The author argues that demolition only moves poverty elsewhere and that upgrading areas where they stand is the more promising approach.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, what usually happens when informal settlements are demolished?
o: Poor families move to another unserviced area, often further from work
Poverty in the city disappears within a few years
Residents receive secure title to new homes
The city lays water pipes along the old lanes
explanation: The second paragraph says demolition more often moves poor families to another unserviced patch of land, usually further from work.

subject: English
q: The passage states that residents who are given secure title to their homes tend to:
o: sell them and return to their villages
demand that the city build new blocks
invest their own savings in improving them
rent them out to newcomers
explanation: Secure title leads residents to invest their savings in stronger walls, better roofs and small businesses.

subject: English
q: The word ‘decree’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: careful planning
public protest
economic growth
an official order
explanation: Growth “cannot be stopped by decree” means an official command cannot halt it; the next sentence recommends planning, so planning is not what is ruled out.

subject: English
q: It can be inferred that the author regards the residents of informal settlements as:
o: essential contributors to the life of the city
a burden the city would be better without
temporary visitors who will soon return home
people unwilling to improve their own homes
explanation: The author notes that these residents are the cooks, drivers, builders and cleaners on whom the rest of the city depends.

subject: English
q: The final paragraph mainly serves to:
o: propose that migration to cities be banned by law
summarise the history of one particular city
argue that planning for growth in advance costs less than repairing damage later
claim that informal settlements cannot be upgraded
explanation: The last paragraph draws the wider lesson that growth cannot be decreed away and that cities which plan ahead spend far less.

subject: English
q: The writer’s main argument is that:
o: new public projects should be abandoned altogether
engineers are responsible for most road accidents
maintaining existing infrastructure deserves a higher priority
private companies should run all public services
explanation: The editorial argues that unnoticed maintenance decides whether infrastructure lasts and that governments should reverse their priorities.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, maintenance budgets are the first to be cut because:
o: engineers prefer to work on new designs
the effects of cutting them are not felt immediately
maintenance costs more than new construction
the law requires new projects to be funded first
explanation: The second paragraph says upkeep budgets are cut first because their absence is not felt immediately.

subject: English
q: Who, according to the writer, suffer most from poor maintenance?
o: Engineers, whose work goes unrewarded
Politicians, who lose elections because of it
Contractors, who lose their building contracts
The poor, who cannot afford private alternatives
explanation: The third paragraph states that those who suffer most are usually the poor, who cannot afford private alternatives.

subject: English
q: The word ‘accumulates’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: disappears slowly
spreads suddenly
builds up gradually
repairs itself
explanation: Damage accumulates silently until a small crack becomes a collapse, so the word means builds up little by little.

subject: English
q: The writer’s remark that a country ‘will keep paying for the same infrastructure twice’ suggests that neglected assets:
o: are usually sold to private owners
must eventually be rebuilt or expensively repaired
earn twice as much revenue as new ones
are replaced by entirely different services
explanation: Because neglect turns small faults into collapses whose bill is many times larger, the public ends up paying again for what it already built.

subject: English
q: The tone of the passage is best described as:
o: bitter and hopeless
critical but constructive
admiring and celebratory
detached and uninterested
explanation: The writer criticises the neglect of upkeep but proposes practical remedies such as a fixed budget share and rewards for engineers.
